title: Countering Domestic Terrorism and Organized Political Violence
summary:
The White House has issued a directive to expand how the government investigates and disrupts domestic terrorism and organized political violence. It orders a nationwide strategy to target not just those who commit violent acts, but also the networks, funding sources, and organizations that support or coordinate them.

Under this plan, federal terrorism task forces will lead investigations into recruiting, radicalization, doxing, swatting, assaults, riots, threats, and property destruction tied to political intimidation. The Justice Department is directed to prosecute relevant crimes to the fullest extent of the law. The Treasury Department will trace money flows and guide banks on spotting suspicious funding, and the tax agency will scrutinize whether any tax-exempt groups are directly or indirectly financing violence. The memo also allows the Attorney General to recommend that certain groups be designated as domestic terrorist organizations and calls for new grant funding to help law enforcement prevent and respond to these threats.

People most likely to benefit include public officials, law enforcement, and everyday citizens who have been targeted by harassment, threats, or violence. Communities that have faced organized political intimidation or destructive unrest may see stronger protection. Financial institutions get clearer direction on what to flag, and agencies gain a more coordinated framework to act before violence occurs.

Those who might be negatively affected include advocacy groups and nonprofits whose activities, funding, or associates come under investigation, especially where protest and civil disobedience border on unlawful conduct. Donors, foundations, and Americans with ties abroad could face greater scrutiny. Civil liberties advocates may worry about overreach, selective enforcement, or chilling effects on speech, association, and protest. Communities already subject to heightened policing and surveillance may feel further pressure. Banks and charities will likely face added compliance burdens. While the memo states actions must remain within the law and available funding, debates over balance—security versus rights—are likely to intensify as this strategy is carried out.
